extracted.intended_audience: readers and scholars of George Washington's writings; historians and students of manners and conduct
extracted.subtask_description: Edition and commentary on George Washington's 'Rules of Civility' — a set of ~110 maxims prescribing behaviour in company, conversation, and at table, together with editorial guidance for reproducing the manuscript.

rubrics_metrics.name: Every action done in company should show respect
rubrics_metrics.description: “Every action done in company ought to be with some sign of respect to those that are present.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied broadly to behaviour in social gatherings: public acts should include a visible sign of reverence or regard for others present. (Text compares Hawkins's longer phrasing and emphasizes Washington's neater restoration of 'respectueux' → 'respect'.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Present seats according to degree
rubrics_metrics.description: “When you present seats let it be to every one according to his degree.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allocate places and deference commensurate with rank/status. The editorial commentary contrasts this succinct Washington phrasing with longer translations; emphasizes observance of social order when seating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not show anger in company (especially at table)
rubrics_metrics.description: If you have reason to be so, Shew it not. (Admonishes not to display anger, including at table.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep temper hidden even if provoked; Hawkins' translation and Washington's phrasing both counsel against showing vexation. Used as an example of refined self-control in public/social settings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstain from laughing at your own witticisms
rubrics_metrics.description: “If you Deliver anything witty and Pleasent abtain from laughing thereat yourself.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When you say something witty, avoid laughing at it yourself; permit others to enjoy it. Washington's curt wording is cited as an improvement in brevity over earlier versions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speak at ordinary volume; affect not to speak louder than usual
rubrics_metrics.description: “Affect not to Speak Louder than ordenary.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not artificially raise your voice for effect or to command attention; maintain normal tone. Presented as one of the maxims Washington retained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain sweetness and mildness; practice moderation
rubrics_metrics.description: Rule 45: 'moderation et douceur' rendered as 'Sweetness and Mildness.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Personal temperament should be moderate, gentle, and mild — a recurring ideal in the maxims. The edition contrasts shorter Washington rendering with longer originals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Never express anything unbecoming or act against moral rules before inferiors
rubrics_metrics.description: “Never express anything unbecoming, nor Act against the Rules Moral before your inferiours.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid immoral or unbecoming speech/acts especially in the presence of those of lower status, since example multiplies culpability. Hawkins' fuller version about multiplying crimes by example is cited as fuller guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not fidget or assume indecorous postures in others' sight
rubrics_metrics.description: “Shift not yourself in the sight of others” — i.e., avoid stretching the body, extending the arms, and assuming different postures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain composed, polite posture in company; the commentary calls the extended original precept 'insufferable impoliteness' to adopt such postures, showing the social importance of bodily restraint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not dispute with superiors; avoid initiating arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: Omit (or avoid) disputing with those of higher rank; Washington's Rule 34 says one ought not to 'begin' with them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not initiate contention with social superiors; the edition contrasts the original's absolute ban on disputing with Washington's softer admonition (do not begin with them), indicating a more measured approach to deference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept reproof gratefully, especially from those on whom you depend
rubrics_metrics.description: Original counsel (partially omitted in Washington's version) advised grateful acceptance of reproof, 'the more if you depend on his authority.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Receive correction with gratitude, particularly from authorities or benefactors. The commentary notes Washington omitted some of the more obsequious language but the principle of accepting correction appears in the tradition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observe proper table manners and service
rubrics_metrics.description: Numerous maxims (and the French source's Chapter XI) address table-setting, service order, use of fork, napkin, toothpick, order of entrees, roasts, salads, dessert (including customs like presenting sugar-plums).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detailed rules govern table conduct, the order of service, and appropriate use of utensils; the introduction quotes the French manual's epicurean chapter as source material and highlights its influence on many Washington maxims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid claiming or exercising privileges of rank (e.g., nearer the fire)
rubrics_metrics.description: The original precept assigned privileges (e.g., approaching nearer the fire, turning one's back) to persons of rank; Washington's version omits or tones down such snobbish precepts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The edition notes Washington's MS generally softens or omits commands that privilege rank, illustrating a subtler, less servile set of rules appropriate to colonial American society.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial reproduction standard: indicate illegible parts and avoid conjectural insertions
rubrics_metrics.description: Dr. J.M. Toner's transcription 'The illegible parts are precisely indicated, without any conjectural insertions, and young Washington's spelling and punctuation subjected to no literary tampering.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When editing/reproducing historical manuscripts: mark illegible text exactly, do not insert conjectural readings, and preserve original spelling/punctuation rather than 'correcting' the author's youthful mistakes. This is presented as best practice followed in the edition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution against excessive abbreviation or over-condensation in transcription
rubrics_metrics.description: Washington's manuscript shows excessive abbreviation; such condensation can sometimes 'deprive maxims of something of their force, if not of their sense.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors should be wary that condensing or omitting material for brevity may weaken the force or clarity of precepts; preserve sufficient wording to retain intended emphasis and meaning.
